l4.transcript:
In November 2021 many countries at the UN annual summit on climate change in Glasgow – the 26th Conference of the Parties (COP26) – made promises to help Earth. They signed agreements to end deforestation and cut methane emission levels by 30 percent by 2030. Presidents of global companies also attended COP26. Jeff Bezos, the founder of Amazon, made a speech on Tuesday. He promised to give \$2 billion to help nature. He said the money would restore landscapes to their more natural state. He also wanted to transform food systems to make food production more sustainable. In 2020, he set up The Bezos Earth Fund. This is a \$10-billion project to help fight climate change. In September 2021, this fund gave \$1 billion to help threatened indigenous peoples.

Jeff Bezos decided to give more money to protect the planet after going into space in July. He said that looking at Earth from space had made him understand the importance of helping our planet. He added: "Looking back at Earth from up there, the atmosphere seems so thin, the world so ... fragile." In his COP26 speech, Mr Bezos claimed his trip into space changed his feelings about our planet. He said: "I was told that seeing Earth from space changes the lens through which you see the world, but I was not prepared for how much that would be true". He insisted that it was time for all countries and corporations to act. He said: "In this critical year ... we must all stand together to protect our world".

This is BBC Europe radio news. We begin with World’s Sport news. German runner, Lukas Jens, has won one of the world’s toughest marathon races retracing the steps of a legendary Greek soldier, who ran from Athens to Sparta. Jens finished the 246 km course from Athens City to Sparta in 24 hours, 20 minutes, and 39 seconds to win for a second year in a row. Frenchman Jean-Jacques Moro came in second with a time of 25 hours, 3 minutes and 30 seconds.

More than 270 runners from some 30 nations took part in this year’s race, which began at the foot of the Acropolis early on Friday morning. Runners were given just 36 hours to complete the route from Athens to Sparta. The modern equivalent of the race was started in 1982 by British soldier John Foden. It takes participants along highways and dirt tracks and over mountains.

Next we turn to the International Book Exhibit in Madrid. Bulgarian publishers and authors together with the National Book Centre are on the road to Spain in order to participate in “Liber”, the twenty third international book exhibit, which takes place from October 12th to October 15th. Bulgaria will be the honoured country at the exhibit this year: 42 Bulgarian publishers and 15 Bulgarian authors will aim to promote Bulgarian literature to the international book markets.

Now, a news item related to a cultural event held in Bulgaria. The Seventh International Puppet Theatre Festival “Puppets and Friends” in Veliko Tarnovo, which started on 10th October, features puppet and mime theatre companies from several European countries. This festival is the only event in Bulgaria to be financed by the Bulgarian Ministry of Culture and the local municipality.

### English Language Course

**Course Programme Specialization:** Offered by Georgia Tech

r2.title: Reading · Task Two
r2.text:
*Read the text below. Then read the questions that follow it and choose the best answer to each question, marking your answers on your answer sheet.*

### Do We Need a Clear-Cut Plan?

Deforestation refers to the destruction of forests. Humans are largely responsible for the loss of forests. The cleared land is used for farming, housing, businesses, mining, and roads. The resources are used for building materials, fuel, medicine, food, and paper. According to some estimates, up to half of the world’s tropical rain forests have already been cleared.

The majority of the earth’s plants and animals live in forests. Deforestation disrupts the food chain. What will happen to the remaining species if we eliminate their natural habitat? We will soon find out.

How did humans let this happen? Survival is the main reason. Converting forests for agricultural purposes is the leading cause of deforestation. Farmers use the cleared land for breeding livestock and planting crops. They rely on the income for survival. Consumers are also to blame. Do you ever think about the trees that were lost so that you could enjoy your daily coffee, tea, rice, or peanuts? We are all contributors to deforestation.

Can the damage be undone? New restrictions on clear-cutting have been introduced in some of the most heavily forested countries. Governments are focusing on reforestation methods and are exploring ways to reverse the damage. Planting mixed forests that are less susceptible to disease is one method of doing this. Learning how to prevent soil erosion is also crucial.

When a tree falls, it decomposes and releases carbon dioxide, methane and other gases into the atmosphere. What does this mean for global warming? According to some scientists, approximately 20% of global carbon emissions result from deforestation. That’s more than the carbon emissions of all vehicles in the world!

r3.title: Reading · Task Three
r3.text:
*Read the text below. Then read the questions that follow it and answer each question with a sentence of your own. Write your answers on your answer sheet. Sentences copied word for word from the text will get 0 points.*

### Bring Your Own Basket!

When an ingenious engineer developed the one-piece, light weight plastic bag for a Swedish company in the 1960s, everybody thought it was a great invention. The plastic bag soon became a convenience that shoppers couldn’t imagine living without. However, as drains and water ways became clogged with plastic, the “single-use” bags were identified as a major environmental threat.

These days, governments around the world are banning plastic bags. In 2002, Bangladesh became the first country to do this. Improper disposal of plastic bags was named as a major contributing factor to devastating floods in Bangladesh in the 1980s and 1990s. The first major US city to impose a plastic bag ban was Los Angeles in 2010. That same year, Mexico City announced a one-billion-dollar annual investment to become a greener city. The Green Plan included a major campaign to scrap the use of plastic bags.

Despite bans and restrictions, the rules are not always enforced in practise. Some shopkeepers complain that they lose money by not offering plastic bags to customers. The opposite occurs in Rwanda, where the nationwide plastic bag ban has been strictly enforced since 2008. Rwanda is one of the cleanest countries in the world due to a mandatory “Clean Up the City” day on the last Saturday of each month. What is more, many shoppers in Rwanda have gone back to the traditional shopping basket.

Not all politicians are in favour of banning plastic bags. In 2012, Toronto Mayor Rob Ford called the idea to scrap plastic bags “dumb” when his city councillors voted to switch from a five-cent fee on plastic bags to an outright ban. Some health experts also agree that it’s not the smartest idea to switch to cloth bags. Reusable bags are typically full of germs. These bags could pose serious health hazards. So do the pros outweigh the cons?
